paragraphs.heading: Mammals that fly
paragraphs.text: Bats make up the order Chiroptera, a name built from Ancient Greek words for "hand" and "wing". They are the only mammals that can truly fly and keep on flying. Each wing is a set of long, spread-out fingers covered by a thin membrane called the patagium. With it, bats move through the air more nimbly than most birds.

paragraphs.heading: A huge family
paragraphs.text: With at least 1,500 known species, bats make up about 20% of every classified mammal species, a total beaten only by rodents. They are found in almost every region of the world. The smallest, Kitti's hog-nosed bat, is 29–33 mm long and weighs 2 g, which makes it one of the tiniest mammals alive. The biggest are the flying foxes: the giant golden-crowned flying fox reaches 1.5 kg and has a wingspan of 1.6 m.

paragraphs.heading: What bats eat
paragraphs.text: Most bats eat insects. Of the rest, most live on fruit or on nectar. A few feed on animals other than insects, and vampire bats feed on blood. Most bats are active at night, and many shelter in caves or other refuges, though nobody is sure whether they do this to escape predators.

paragraphs.heading: Why bats matter
paragraphs.text: In their ecosystems, bats pollinate flowers, spread seeds and keep insect numbers in check. By eating insect pests they cut the need for pesticides, and their dung, called guano, has been dug out of caves to use as fertiliser. Bats can draw tourists, and people in Africa, Asia, the Pacific and the Caribbean eat them. They are also a natural home for many disease-causing pathogens such as rabies, and because they are mobile, social and long-lived, they pass disease among themselves easily. That becomes a danger when people interact with them.

paragraphs.heading: Traces in stone
paragraphs.text: Bat skeletons are delicate and do not fossilise well; only about 12% of the bat genera that ever lived are thought to have turned up as fossils. The oldest known bat fossils, from 55–56 million years ago, are nothing but isolated teeth. The oldest complete skeletons, 52 million years old, were found in Wyoming. Two bats from the Messel Pit in Germany, 48 million years old, were the first fossil mammals whose colour was discovered: both were reddish-brown.

paragraphs.heading: Flight came first
paragraphs.text: One of the Wyoming bats, Onychonycteris finneyi, found in 2003, shows that flight evolved before the ability to echolocate. Unlike bats today, it had claws on all five fingers, and its longer hind legs and shorter forearms may have helped it climb. Its short, broad wings suggest its flights were slower and shorter than those of later bats. Genome studies strongly back the idea that all bats share common ancestry and that flight arose just once in mammals.
